summary: Specifies the Link Management Protocol, which runs between a pair of nodes to manage traffic engineering links. Multiple data links can be combined into a single TE link, and management can use out-of-band techniques. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: LMP lets two neighboring network nodes coordinate their control connection and the data links they manage. It can check which links connect, compare their descriptions, and report failures.

questions: how does lmp verify data links
what is a control channel in lmp
subtitle: How neighboring nodes coordinate control channels, verify their data links, and report link failures.

tldr.problem: A pair of network nodes may share many data links while their control messages travel over a separate path. The nodes need to check the control path and manage the data links independently.
tldr.mechanism: LMP negotiates and checks control channels, compares link descriptions, can test data-link connectivity, and carries status reports between neighbors.
tldr.outcome: LMP defines shared procedures for managing traffic-engineering links. RFC 4204 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6898.

today: RFC 4204 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2005. It has been updated by RFC 6898.

sections.title: Why Link Management Is Needed
sections.content:
RFC 4204 defines the Link Management Protocol (LMP) for a pair of neighboring nodes. Several data links can be grouped into one traffic-engineering (TE) link, and the control path between the nodes may use a different physical network from those data links.

That separation means a working control channel does not prove that the data links work, and a working data link does not prove that the control channel works. LMP covers control-channel connectivity, agreement on link properties, optional data-link verification, and optional fault management.
sections.plainLanguage: LMP manages the links between two neighboring network nodes. The control connection and the links carrying traffic can fail independently, so LMP checks and reports them separately.

sections.title: Setting Up and Checking a Control Channel
sections.content:
A control channel is a pair of mutually reachable IP interfaces. Each node assigns it a unique, non-zero 32-bit control-channel identifier. LMP sends its messages over UDP; the RFC assigns LMP port 701.

Nodes exchange Config messages to agree on channel parameters and answer with ConfigAck or ConfigNack. They can then exchange Hello messages as keep-alives. The HelloDeadInterval must exceed the HelloInterval and should be at least three times as large; suggested directly connected defaults are 150 ms and 500 ms.

If all control channels fail while data links still carry traffic, the TE link can remain in a Degraded state. The RFC says routing and signaling should be told not to accept new connections on that link.
sections.plainLanguage: The nodes first agree on control-channel settings. They then exchange regular Hello messages; if those stop, they treat the channel as failed.

sections.title: Agreeing on the Link Properties
sections.content:
The LinkSummary exchange lets neighbors compare how they describe a TE link and its data links. A summary carries the local and remote link identifiers, the list of component data links, and properties such as support for verification or fault management.

The receiving node sends LinkSummaryAck when the descriptions agree, or LinkSummaryNack when they do not. Identifiers at both ends must use the same type, such as IPv4, IPv6, or unnumbered. The exchange should happen before the link is brought up.
sections.plainLanguage: Each node sends its description of the shared link. The other node confirms the description or reports which details do not match.

sections.title: Testing Data-Link Connectivity
sections.content:
Link verification is optional. It checks whether data links physically connect and can discover which interface at one node connects to which interface at the other. The RFC recommends using it when setting up a TE link and periodically for unallocated data links.

The nodes coordinate with BeginVerify messages over a control channel. After the peer accepts, the initiator sends Test messages over each data link. The receiver reports success or failure over the control channel, and the initiator acknowledges that status. Test is the only LMP message that must travel over a data link.

For transparent devices, a link must be made opaque during testing so the Test message can be detected. Once the links have been tested, EndVerify closes the procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: The nodes agree to test a data link, then one sends a Test message over it. The other reports whether it received that message over the control channel.

sections.title: Reporting and Locating Failures
sections.content:
Fault management is optional and is negotiated for each TE link. LMP does not prescribe how a node detects a fault; it carries reports after a fault has been detected, for example by a physical-layer signal monitor.

A downstream node reports failed data links to its upstream neighbor with ChannelStatus. The upstream node acknowledges the report and checks whether it also sees the failure. If it does not, the failure is localized to the link between the two nodes. A node can request status if it has not received a report.
sections.plainLanguage: A node reports a failed data link to its upstream neighbor. The neighbor checks its own side to determine whether the failure lies between them.

sections.title: Reliable Messages and Restart Recovery
sections.content:
LMP messages that require reliable delivery carry a monotonically increasing Message_Id and are acknowledged with that identifier. A sender retransmits an unacknowledged message with an increasing delay until it receives an acknowledgment or reaches its retry limit. Suggested defaults are an initial 500 ms interval, a doubling interval, and a retry limit of 3.

After a control-plane restart, a node sets the LMP Restart flag until a Hello confirms that its neighbor has seen the restart. The neighbor then sends a LinkSummary for each TE link so the nodes can restore their link descriptions and learn which data links are allocated.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages that need confirmation are numbered and resent if no acknowledgment arrives. After a restart, the nodes exchange link summaries to restore their shared link information.

sections.title: The Common Message Header
sections.content:
LMP messages share a common header followed by LMP objects. The header contains a 4-bit version field, flags, an 8-bit message type, and a 16-bit message length, along with reserved fields. Version 1 is defined by this RFC, and values are encoded in network byte order.

The two defined flags are ControlChannelDown and LMP Restart. Objects have their own headers and carry identifiers, configuration values, status, or other message data. LMP message types include Config, Hello, Test, LinkSummary, and ChannelStatus.
sections.plainLanguage: Each LMP message starts with fields that identify its version, purpose, and length. Objects after the header carry the details for that message.

sections.title: Protecting LMP Control Traffic
sections.content:
The RFC identifies spoofed, modified, and replayed control packets as possible attacks. LMP security must provide authentication, integrity, and replay protection; the RFC says confidentiality is not needed for LMP control traffic and Test messages on data links do not need protection.

Where security is needed, implementations should use IPsec. ESP with trailer authentication in tunnel mode must be supported, and IKE must be used when peers negotiate keys dynamically. Manual keying cannot provide replay protection or automatic re-keying and is recommended only for diagnostics.
sections.plainLanguage: Control messages need protection against forgery, changes, and replay. The RFC specifies IPsec support for that protection.
